lead: This unit teaches the gates that act on qubits and the circuits built from them. You will learn single- and multi-qubit gates, universality, the circuit model, no-cloning, teleportation, superdense coding, and how to run circuits in Qiskit. After it you can read a quantum circuit, compute its output state, and write and simulate a small circuit.
about: This unit is the hardware-free heart of quantum computing: the gates and circuits that turn qubits into computations. Chapter 3.1 defines the single-qubit Pauli, Hadamard and phase gates as matrices and actions. Chapter 3.2 adds CNOT, SWAP and Toffoli, the gates that create entanglement. Chapter 3.3 explains why a small gate set is universal, and Chapter 3.4 assembles gates into the circuit model. Chapter 3.5 proves the no-cloning theorem, which limits copying. Chapters 3.6 and 3.7 use shared Bell pairs for teleportation and superdense coding. Chapter 3.8 puts the same circuits into Qiskit and a simulator. The order matters: each chapter uses the gates and circuits built before it.

chapters.idea: A single qubit is changed by a 2×2 unitary matrix, and the Pauli, Hadamard and phase gates are the standard building blocks.
chapters.depth: Define the 2×2 unitary matrix of each gate and its action on |0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩ and |−⟩. Cover Pauli X (NOT, bit flip), Y (bit and phase flip), Z (phase flip), Hadamard H (some syllabi call it Walsh-Hadamard), phase gates S (π/2), T (π/4), and the general phase gate P(φ). Show H²=I, X²=I, Z²=I, S²=Z, T²=S. Give the Bloch-sphere picture: X, Y, Z are π rotations; H is a half-turn about the diagonal. Keep global phase out of measurement probabilities. State clearly that every gate is unitary and reversible.

figure.title: Matrix entries, row by row
figure.aria: A table of 2×2 matrix entries for the Pauli gates, Hadamard and the S gate, with the four entries of each matrix read row by row.

chapters.example: Start with |0⟩. Apply H, then Z, then H. Find the final state and the probability of measuring 0. Solution: H|0⟩=|+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2; Z|+⟩=|−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2; H|−⟩=|1⟩. The final state is |1⟩, so P(0)=0 and P(1)=1.
chapters.trap: Order matters: the rightmost gate acts first. Z flips the phase, not the bit, and H is not a NOT gate. H is self-inverse, so HH=I.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: matrices and unitary matrices. Unit 2: qubit states, superposition, Bloch sphere and measurement.
chapters.leave: Two-qubit gates and entanglement go to 3.2. The full measurement postulate goes to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Controlled gates act on one qubit only when another qubit is 1, and CNOT is the standard gate for making entanglement.
chapters.depth: Cover CNOT (controlled-X): control a, target b, b→b⊕a. Give its 4×4 matrix in the basis |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩. Cover SWAP, which exchanges two qubits and is built from three CNOTs. Cover Toffoli (CCNOT), which flips the target only when both controls are 1. Mention Fredkin (controlled-SWAP), which some syllabi list next to Toffoli. Give truth tables and circuit symbols. Show that H on one qubit followed by CNOT creates a Bell state. Verify the SWAP construction on a basis state.

figure.title: SWAP from three CNOTs
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain showing that three CNOT gates, with the middle one reversed, swap two qubits.

chapters.example: Start with |01⟩. Apply CNOT(1→2), then CNOT(2→1), then CNOT(1→2). Show the state after each step and the final state. Solution: CNOT(1→2) leaves |01⟩ because q1=0; CNOT(2→1) flips q1 because q2=1, giving |11⟩; CNOT(1→2) flips q2 because q1=1, giving |10⟩. The result is |10⟩, the original qubits swapped.
chapters.trap: CNOT is not SWAP, and two opposite CNOTs do not swap. Toffoli needs both controls equal to 1, not either one. Track control and target labels.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for single-qubit gates and matrix forms. Unit 2 for tensor-product order and Bell states.
chapters.leave: Universality proofs go to 3.3. Bell-state applications go to 3.6, 3.7 and Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A small finite set of gates can build any quantum circuit to any required accuracy, so hardware only needs a few gate types.
chapters.depth: A gate set is universal if any unitary on n qubits can be built to accuracy ε using gates from the set. State the standard result: single-qubit gates plus CNOT are universal. Give {H, T, CNOT} as a finite universal set, called Clifford+T. Explain exact versus approximate universality. State that Clifford gates {H, S, CNOT} alone are not universal. Some syllabi say universal logic gates or two-level unitary gates; mention that any unitary is a product of two-level unitaries. Mention Solovay-Kitaev only as a name for gate-count bounds, and say only a few universities teach it in detail.

figure.title: Approximating any unitary
figure.aria: A downward flowchart showing an arbitrary unitary decomposed into two-qubit gates, then single-qubit gates, then H and T gates, with final error at most epsilon.

chapters.example: Show how to build X from H and T, allowing an overall global phase. Solution: T⁴ = −Z, so H T⁴ H = H(−Z)H = −X. The circuit H, T, T, T, T, H gives X up to the global phase −1, which no measurement can see.
chapters.trap: Clifford gates alone are not universal. Approximate means error ≤ ε, not exact. Global phase cannot be observed and should not be counted as an error.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 and 3.2 for the gate matrices and CNOT. Unit 1 for unitary matrices and matrix products.
chapters.leave: Full algorithm design goes to Unit 4. Fault-tolerant gate constructions go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A quantum circuit is a sequence of unitary gates on wires followed by measurements, and its output is computed by multiplying matrices in reverse gate order.
chapters.depth: Define wires, gates, measurement and the left-to-right reading convention. Define width (number of qubits) and depth (longest path of gates). Explain composition: if gate A is followed by gate B, the matrix is BA. Show a Bell-state circuit and its 4×4 unitary. Give simple circuit identities such as HZH=X and CNOT identities. State that the circuit model is equivalent to other models of quantum computation. Some syllabi call this the quantum circuit model of computation and circuit development. Keep design small: two to three qubits.

figure.title: Bell-state circuit
figure.aria: A left-to-right pipeline starting from two qubits in state 00, applying H to the first qubit, then CNOT, then measurement.

chapters.example: Build (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 from |00⟩ using H on q0 and then CNOT(q0→q1). Write the state after H and after CNOT, and give the measurement probabilities. Solution: after H, (|00⟩+|10⟩)/√2; after CNOT, (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2; measuring gives 00 with probability 1/2 and 11 with probability 1/2.
chapters.trap: The first gate on the left is applied last in matrix multiplication. Fix the wire order, usually |q0 q1⟩. Measurement collapses the state and destroys superposition.
chapters.prereq: 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 for gates and universality. Unit 2 for tensor products and measurement.
chapters.leave: Algorithm-specific circuits go to Unit 4. Qiskit syntax goes to 3.8. No-cloning is proved in 3.5.

chapters.idea: No physical process can copy an arbitrary unknown quantum state, because a universal copier would violate linearity.
chapters.depth: Give the proof by linearity and inner product. Suppose U copies every state: U(|ψ⟩|0⟩)=|ψ⟩|ψ⟩. For |0⟩ and |1⟩ this forces U|00⟩=|00⟩ and U|10⟩=|11⟩. For |+⟩, linearity gives (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, while a clone would be |+⟩|+⟩=(|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)/2. The inner product of the two outputs is 1/√2, not 1, so no such U exists. State that orthogonal states can be copied, known states can be prepared, and no-cloning supports QKD security. Some syllabi list this under quantum computational complexity—no cloning theorem, but complexity classes belong to Unit 4.

figure.title: Why a universal cloner fails
figure.aria: A downward flowchart starting from a supposed universal cloner, showing its action on 0 and 1, then linearity on a superposition, ending in a state that is not a clone.

chapters.example: Try to clone |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 with a cloner that copies |0⟩ and |1⟩. Compare the linearity output with the required clone and compute the inner product. Solution: linearity gives (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2; the clone is (|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)/2; their inner product is 1/√2, so they cannot be the same state.
chapters.trap: CNOT copies computational basis states only; it does not clone a superposition. No-cloning does not forbid teleportation, because teleportation destroys the original.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 and 3.2 for superposition and CNOT. Unit 2 for inner products and Bell states.
chapters.leave: QKD security proofs go to Unit 5. Complexity classes such as BQP go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Teleportation sends an unknown qubit from Alice to Bob using one shared Bell pair and two classical bits, without copying it.
chapters.depth: Give the protocol. Alice and Bob share |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2. Alice holds |ψ⟩=α|0⟩+β|1⟩. She applies CNOT(q0→q1), then H on q0, then measures both qubits. She sends the two bits m1m2 to Bob. Bob applies I for 00, X for 01, Z for 10, and XZ for 11. Derive the four-term state and the correction table. Emphasise that the original is destroyed, one ebit and two classical bits are used, and no signal travels faster than light.

figure.title: Teleportation and corrections
figure.aria: A downward flowchart: Alice performs a Bell measurement on the unknown qubit and her half of a Bell pair, the two outcome bits choose one of four corrections I, X, Z or XZ, and Bob then holds the original state.

chapters.example: Teleport |ψ⟩=(3/5)|0⟩+(4/5)|1⟩ using a shared |Φ+⟩. Write the state after Alice's CNOT and H, and give Bob's gate for each measurement outcome m1m2. Solution: the state is ½[|00⟩((3/5)|0⟩+(4/5)|1⟩) + |01⟩((3/5)|1⟩+(4/5)|0⟩) + |10⟩((3/5)|0⟩−(4/5)|1⟩) + |11⟩((3/5)|1⟩−(4/5)|0⟩)]. Bob applies I for 00, X for 01, Z for 10, XZ for 11.
chapters.trap: Alice's measurement destroys |ψ⟩, so this is not copying. Bob needs both classical bits before choosing the correction. Teleportation is not faster-than-light.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for CNOT. 3.4 for circuits. Unit 2 for Bell states and measurement.
chapters.leave: Bell inequality experiments go to Unit 2. QKD goes to Unit 5. Superdense coding is 3.7.

chapters.idea: With a shared Bell pair, sending one qubit can carry two classical bits.
chapters.depth: Give the protocol. Alice and Bob share |Φ+⟩. Alice chooses two bits and applies I for 00, X for 01, Z for 10, or XZ for 11 to her qubit. She sends her qubit to Bob. Bob applies CNOT and then H, and measures both qubits to read the two bits. Derive the encoding table and show the decode for one case. State the resources: one ebit shared beforehand, one qubit sent, two classical bits received. Mention that this is the dual of teleportation.

figure.title: Encoding table: bits to gate to Bell state
figure.aria: A four-row table mapping the two classical bits 00, 01, 10 and 11 to the gates I, X, Z and XZ and to the resulting Bell states.

chapters.example: Alice wants to send bits 10 using a shared |Φ+⟩. Which gate does she apply, what state does Bob receive, and what does Bob measure after CNOT and H? Solution: apply Z, giving (|00⟩−|11⟩)/√2. Bob's CNOT and H map this to |10⟩, so he reads 10.
chapters.trap: Without the shared Bell pair, one qubit carries at most one classical bit. The bits are not sent as classical signals. Memorise the encoding table in the right order.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for CNOT. 3.4 for circuits. Unit 2 for Bell states.
chapters.leave: Channel capacity and QKD go to Unit 5. Teleportation is 3.6.

chapters.idea: Qiskit turns a circuit diagram into code that can be simulated or run on a quantum processor.
chapters.depth: Cover the Qiskit workflow: QuantumCircuit, h(), cx(), measure(), StatevectorSampler or AerSimulator, transpile, run with shots, and counts. Show a Bell-state program and explain bitstring order: Qiskit prints the highest-index qubit on the left. Distinguish exact statevector simulation from sampled counts, and simulator from noisy hardware. Mention that Qiskit is an IBM open-source tool. Say only a few universities teach hardware job submission in detail. Keep algorithms out of this chapter.

figure.title: Qiskit workflow
figure.aria: A left-to-right pipeline from creating a two-qubit circuit, adding H and CNOT, measuring both qubits, running 1024 shots on a simulator, to counts near 512 for 00 and 512 for 11.

chapters.example: Write a Qiskit circuit for a Bell state on 2 qubits, measure both qubits, and run 1024 shots on a simulator. State the expected counts. Solution: apply h(0) and cx(0,1), measure, and run 1024 shots. The ideal counts are about 512 for 00 and 512 for 11; real hardware gives noisy counts near these values.
chapters.trap: Qiskit bitstrings put the highest-index qubit on the left. Counts are statistical, not exact. Forgetting measure() gives no counts.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 for the circuit model. 3.2 for CNOT. Unit 2 for measurement probabilities.
chapters.leave: Hardware calibration and error mitigation go to Unit 5. Variational algorithms go to Unit 6.
